diagnostic_evidence.quote: Now let us analyze the equality case. In terms of matrix $M$, it can be achieved only if $M$ is non-negative (but not positive).
These three rows form the three $2 \times 2$ submatrices of $\hat{C}$ with the smallest singular value equal to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}}$.
which finalizes the proof of the equality criteria.

issues.failure_explanation: The proposition asserts a biconditional, but the equality analysis only derives the clustering from an assumed equality: assuming the best bound is attained, it deduces M ≥ 0 with a zero entry, λ1(G)=λ2(G)=2/n, the three-block factorization of M, and reads off magnitudes and collinearity. The converse — that a matrix clustered as described attains best inverse exactly √n, i.e. that no 2×2 submatrix has σ2 > 1/√n (equivalently, that a clustered matrix has M in the block form (blck)) — is never verified. The Case A step 'These three rows form the three 2×2 submatrices of Ĉ with the smallest singular value equal to 1/√(n−1)' relies precisely on this unproved extremality content.

failure_location.quote: The corresponding equality is achieved if and only if the rows of the matrix are clustered into three non-empty groups of $p, \, q, \, r > 0$ pairwise collinear vectors, with the squared magnitudes equal to $\frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{2p}$, $\frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{2q}$ and $\frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{2r}$, respectively.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the missing verification: for a clustered matrix (rows ±√(1/(2n)+1/(2k_g)) along the three lines determined by Σ k_g s_g P(θ_g) = I), compute M and show it equals the block form (blck) (cross-block entries 0); then every within-group submatrix is singular and every cross-group pair satisfies P(1/n) = 0, i.e. σ2 = 1/√n exactly, proving the 'if' direction and the extremality of the representative cross-pairs.
issues.overall_effect: The 'if' direction of the equality characterization in Proposition pr, and the matching claim 2 of Corollary co, are unsupported; the identification of the extremal submatrices of an equality-case matrix, used inside Case A, is likewise ungrounded.
issues.title: Equality criterion of Proposition pr is proved only in the 'only if' direction
issues.why_classification: The gap is closed by a contained computation (block form of M for clustered matrices plus the identity λ2 = 1/n for cross pairs); no advertised claim, rate or regime is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $v_1, v_2, v_3 \in \mathds{R}^2$ be vectors with pairwise non-collinear squares. Then the three $2 \times 2$ matrices composed of these vectors as rows have pairwise different first (and second) right-singular vectors.
Thus, the conjugated square of the first right-singular vector is oriented as the sum of the squares of vectors $v_i$ and $v_j$.
By Lemma \ref{le} vector $(\pm 1, 0)^T$ can be a right-singular vector of at most one of these three submatrices.

issues.failure_explanation: The final inference of the proof is false, and with it the lemma's statement. Counterexample: squares w1 = (1,0), w2 = (0,1), w3 = (1,2) are pairwise non-collinear (realized by rows (1,0), 2^{-1/2}(1,1) and ≈(1.272, 0.786)); yet w1 + w2 = (1,1) and w1 + w3 = (2,2) are collinear, and by the proof's own formula the square of the first right singular vector points along the sum of the row squares, so the matrices [v1;v2] and [v1;v3] share their first right singular vector (direct computation: the top eigenvector of A^TA has direction (1, √2−1), angle 22.5°, for both). Each matrix has distinct singular values, so the conclusion 'pairwise different first right-singular vectors' genuinely fails.

failure_location.quote: Since $v_1^2$, $v_2^2$ and $v_3^2$ are pairwise non-collinear, their sums $v_1^2 + v_2^2$, $v_1^2 + v_3^2$ and $v_2^2 + v_3^2$ are pairwise non-collinear too, which finalizes the proof of the lemma.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the lemma by the restricted assertion actually needed and true in the application: in the equality-case configuration (three groups with Σ k_g ŵ_g = 0 and |ŵ_g| = 1/(2m)+1/(2k_g)) at most one of the three representative sums ŵ_g + ŵ_h is a negative real number, i.e. at most one representative pair has (±1,0) as σ2-right-singular vector; prove it from the constraint by a contained case analysis on imaginary/real parts.
issues.overall_effect: The Case A step 'By Lemma le vector (±1,0)^T can be a right-singular vector of at most one of these three submatrices' is unsound, so the strictness argument excluding equality for matrices with a small row — and with it the necessity direction of Proposition pr's criterion and Corollary co — is unproven.
issues.title: Lemma le is false: sums of pairwise non-collinear squares can be collinear
issues.why_classification: The replacement is an elementary but genuinely multi-case argument; the paper's main statements remain true and provable, only the auxiliary lemma is abandoned in its stated generality.

issues.failure_explanation: With t = 1/(1−b²) the first column of Ĉ = C·diag(t,1) has squared norm t²(1−b²) = 1/(1−b²) ≠ 1, so Ĉ is not orthonormal and the inductive hypothesis (stated for matrices with orthonormal columns) is invoked outside its hypotheses. The identity used in (ineq), 1/t² = 1−b², is also false for the printed t (1/t² = (1−b²)²), so the chain ending at σ2² ≥ 1/n is not established. The normalization consistent with the rest of the argument is t = (1−b²)^{−1/2}, for which Ĉ is orthonormal and (ineq) holds; the equality condition '(i) b = 1/n' should then read b² = 1/n.

failure_location.quote: Multiplying its first column by $t = \frac{1}{1 - b^2} > 1$ we get the orthogonal matrix

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Redefine t = (1−b²)^{−1/2} (then Ĉ^TĈ = I and 1/t² = 1−b²) and read condition (i) as b² = 1/n; all subsequent estimates and the equality analysis hold verbatim.
issues.overall_effect: Case A of the proof of Proposition pr (the bound and its strictness for matrices with a row of norm ≤ 1/√n) is unsound as written; Corollary co, derived from the proposition, is affected transitively.
issues.title: Wrong column-scaling factor t = 1/(1−b²) in Case A: Ĉ is not orthonormal
issues.why_classification: A local redefinition of one constant repairs the construction and the estimate; every substantive claim and guarantee survives unchanged.
